name: Mikado Orange
lede: Mikado Orange is a strong, warm orange plated twice by Ridgway in 1912 and echoed in RAL's industrial list, sharing its name but not its hue with the duller [[mikado-brown|Mikado Brown]].

sections.title: One name, two Ridgway plates
sections.body:
Ridgway's atlas records this hue twice: at plate III, hue 13, tone b, and again at plate II, hue 11, tone b, both from 1912 [1]. The ISCC-NBS system of 1955 classifies it as a moderate orange, about 4.7 units from that block's reference chip, and RAL's industrial list carries a near-duplicate chip, RAL 2012, close enough that our library flags it a near-duplicate within about 2 units [1][2]. As with Mikado Brown, Ridgway offers no stated reason for the name beyond the title itself [1].

Its nearest library neighbor is [[faded-orange|Faded Orange]], and it sits close to [[tangerine|Tangerine]] and [[alloy-orange|Alloy Orange]] on the same warm-orange stretch of the chart [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of Mikado Orange covers at least five per cent of the canvas in only 5 works, as photographed [3]. The earliest is Lucas Cranach the Elder's *Adam* from 1528, and it is otherwise over-represented in paintings from Germany and the United States and functions purely as a highlight color [3]. Its rarity against Mikado Brown's one-in-eighteen presence shows how differently two colors with the same borrowed name can behave [3]. These remain photographs of aged, varnished canvases read as screen colors, not pigment tests [3].
